tldr: The authors developed 4DSynth, a system that procedurally generates fully editable 4D simulation environments—complete with animated actors and physics—from text, floor plan masks, or a single photograph, revealing the limitations of state-of-the-art VLMs on navigation tasks.
hero_caption: Overall pipeline of 4DSynth. User instructions are parsed to construct scene geometry through one of four routes. On a shared Stage, dynamic actor trajectories and camera paths are then planned with geometric consistency before being exported to a simulator.
overview:
Training embodied AI agents to navigate household environments requires settings that are not only visually diverse, but also dynamic, with moving obstacles and physical interactivity. However, manual environment authoring is prohibitively expensive. Recent video and 4D generative AI models look compelling visually, but they lack physical entities—such as colliders and editable parameters—that robots can actually interact with.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed 4DSynth, an end-to-end 4D world synthesis pipeline grounded in procedural generation. From diverse inputs such as natural-language instructions, floor plan masks, or a single room photograph, 4DSynth routes through a shared internal representation called the Stage. This enables one-stop generation of simulation spaces where collision meshes, walkable surfaces, and animated humans maintain full geometric consistency.

To demonstrate its utility, the authors automatically constructed 4DSynth-Nav, an interactive benchmark featuring 333 navigation and manipulation tasks with dynamic pedestrians across 122 physics-ready indoor scenes. Evaluating two state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs), Qwen3-VL and Gemini 3.1 Pro, showed that even top-tier Gemini achieved only a 33.3% success rate. The benchmark exposed how errors accumulate and cause agents to stall when targets lie outside the initial field of view or when tasks involve multiple stages.
contributions: A procedural synthesis architecture that unifies diverse input routes—such as text, blueprint masks, and single photos—into a shared internal geometric representation called the Stage.

A geometry-grounded 4D synthesis pipeline that automatically plans collision-free trajectories for actors and cameras based on real asset measurements, exporting physics-ready OpenUSD scenes for Isaac Sim.
The construction of 4DSynth-Nav, a fully automated benchmark consisting of 333 tasks with dynamic obstacles, along with a systematic failure analysis of frontier VLM agents.

sections.heading: Why do embodied robots need editable 4D environments?
sections.summary: Building training environments that combine visual diversity, physical structure, and temporal dynamics (4D) has historically required piecing together fragmented tools. 4DSynth introduces an integrated system that consistently produces editable, physics-ready 4D worlds from diverse inputs.
sections.details:
For embodied robots to operate intelligently in the real world, simulators must offer realistic visuals, structural diversity across rooms, and dynamic elements such as moving people. Previously, however, layout generators, text-to-scene tools, and human motion platforms existed as disconnected silos. Bringing them together into a single, editable scene was extraordinarily difficult.

In this work, a "4D environment" does not merely mean rendering moving pixels. It means an environment with explicit 3D geometry coupled with time-varying actor and camera states. By explicitly retaining geometry, object colliders, support relations (what sits on top of what), and procedural parameters remain fully intact all the way through rendering and physics simulation.

The system relies on an agentic controller to interpret user text prompts and build a shared Stage through four generation routes. It then plans character animations and camera trajectories directly on top of that geometry, ultimately exporting OpenUSD assets ready for execution in platforms like Isaac Sim.

sections.heading: How does 4DSynth differ from existing simulators and 4D generative AI?
sections.summary: Existing work has focused on platforms using fixed, static assets or visual-only 4D generation that lacks interactivity. 4DSynth is novel in unifying procedural editability, geometric consistency, dynamic human actors, and physical simulation in one pipeline.
sections.details:
Simulation platforms for robotics—such as AI2-THOR, Habitat, iGibson, and SAPIEN—primarily focus on executing tasks across pre-existing scene collections rather than synthesizing full environments flexibly from scratch.

Procedural systems like ProcTHOR and Infinigen, as well as LLM-driven scene generators like Holodeck, have also emerged. However, 4DSynth tackles system-level integration: it bridges disparate input routes (native synthesis, floor plans, single images) while maintaining geometric consistency for both dynamic actors and moving cameras.

Furthermore, recent text-to-4D methods based on NeRFs or 3D Gaussian Splatting generate realistic video, but they do not provide walkable floor meshes, rigid-body collision, or downstream parameter editing. By intentionally mapping to explicit objects and procedural assets, 4DSynth trades photorealistic pixel-matching to prioritize interactability and editability for embodied agents.

sections.heading: The 4DSynth architecture: From raw input to physics simulation
sections.summary: The system derives a shared geometric Stage from four generation routes and optimizes character and camera trajectories over it. Finally, it calculates mass and friction from procedural materials to export physics-ready scenes for Isaac Sim.
sections.details:
4DSynth is organized into three tiers: semantic control, scene realization, and geometry-grounded 4D synthesis (Figure F2).

■ III-A Controllable Scene Synthesis
Scenes are generated through two main avenues spanning four routes. The first is native synthesis, which produces rooms or expansive outdoor scenes across 8 biomes from simple category prompts. The second compiles external inputs: generating from text or floor plan masks (Figure F3), and a "Real-to-Sim" route from a single photograph (Figure F4). For photos, monocular depth and segmentation estimate 3D proxies, which are then mapped to procedural assets to freeze geometry before matching materials and colors to the source image. For outdoor scenes, a coarse-to-fine loop plans tentative actor trajectories on rough terrain before generating camera-visible details.

■ III-B 4D Animation on the Shared Stage
A Stage is extracted from the generated geometry, providing a heightfield and a walkable region $\mathcal{W}$. For an actor $i$ with body radius $r_i$, the system erodes the walkable area into $\mathcal{F}_i = \operatorname{Erode}(\mathcal{W}, r_i)$, and runs $A^*$ to plan collision-free paths. Actors receive realistic human heights and walking speeds, and multiple actors navigate around one another.

■ III-C Geometrically Consistent Observation Synthesis
Director intent (panning, orbiting, zooming) is decoupled from physical constraints. The camera trajectory is adjusted via strict or fast collision modes to prevent clipping into walls or actors, while optimizing framing to keep subjects centered.

■ III-D Exporting to Physics Simulation
The finished 4D scene is converted into OpenUSD format for NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Density and friction coefficients are derived automatically from procedural material properties, and rigid-body colliders are assigned to movable objects. Pedestrians are treated as kinematic capsule obstacles that trace their planned paths.

sections.heading: Qualitative scene generation and 333 navigation benchmark tasks
sections.summary: Generated environments faithfully follow floor plan layouts and remain fully editable. When evaluating frontier VLMs on the automated 4DSynth-Nav benchmark, even the best model reached only a 33.3% success rate.
sections.details:
■ IV-A Qualitative Scene Synthesis Results
Generating from floor plan masks (Figure F5) accurately respects 2D layout constraints while producing realistic 3D rooms with customized lighting and furniture. For single-image inputs (Figure F6), 4DSynth preserves walls, openings, and secondary props far more reliably than prior work like VIGA, while remaining fully editable. Figure F7 demonstrates collision-free actor walking and natural camera paths in both indoor and outdoor settings.

■ IV-B & IV-C 4DSynth-Nav Benchmark Construction and Difficulty Tiers
The authors procedurally generated 333 navigation and pick-and-place tasks across 122 physics-ready indoor scenes without human intervention, incorporating walking humans as dynamic obstacles. Difficulty spans three tiers defined along two axes (subtask count and initial target visibility): L1 (1-stage, target invisible initially), L2 (2-stage, target visible initially), and L3 (2-stage, target invisible initially).

■ IV-D & IV-E Experimental Setup and Results
Two VLM agents were evaluated: Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B-Thinking and Gemini 3.1 Pro. Agents received first-person visual observations alongside text prompts and planned actions up to 5 steps ahead.
Qwen3-VL achieved an overall Success Rate (SR) of only 13.2% (Subtask Progress SP: 22.4%), while Gemini 3.1 Pro achieved an SR of 33.3% (SP: 40.7%). While Gemini demonstrated strong exploration in L1 (57.5% SR with invisible targets), its performance plummeted to 18.2% SR on the 2-stage L3 tasks.

■ IV-F Trajectory Analysis
Both models exhibited a steep drop from subtask progress to overall success. As shown in Figure 8, agents often reached their first target, but failed to recognize state transitions upon entering the second stage. This led to error compounding, where agents detoured away from the goal and timed out.

sections.heading: Conclusions and future outlook
sections.summary: 4DSynth establishes a practical pipeline that generates editable, physics-ready 4D worlds from diverse inputs. Future work will explore reactive human actors that yield to robots, articulated furniture, and evaluations across a broader range of embodied agents.
sections.details:
This work presented 4DSynth, a system that generates editable 4D environments with dynamic characters from natural language, floor plans, or single photos. Unifying generation through a shared Stage and WorldState eliminates manual 3D modeling while seamlessly bridging rendering, physics simulation, and automated task generation.

Furthermore, experiments on the newly generated 4DSynth-Nav benchmark proved that even frontier VLMs experience substantial performance drops when challenged by dynamic obstacles, multi-stage goals, and targets outside the initial field of view.

The authors outline several directions for future work: further quantifying input fidelity and controllability, implementing interactive human actors that actively yield path rights to robots, and expanding articulated objects such as functional drawers and doors.

takeaways: Shifting from visual 4D to physics-ready, editable 4D: Unlike appearance-driven approaches like NeRFs or Gaussian Splatting, procedural worlds with explicit geometry are essential for robotics.

The power of a shared representation (Stage): Consolidating text, blueprint, and image inputs into a single geometric stage with collision and walkability data allows downstream animation and camera planning to share one universal pipeline.

Where frontier VLMs stand today: Even cutting-edge models like Gemini 3.1 Pro succeed less than 20% of the time on 2-stage tasks with dynamic obstacles and invisible targets, highlighting major hurdles for real-world deployment.
limitations: Lack of human-robot interaction: Currently, walking pedestrians follow pre-baked kinematic trajectories and do not pause, swerve, or yield when an embodied agent approaches.
Limited furniture articulation: Physics-based articulation mechanisms for everyday assets, such as opening cabinet doors and pulling out drawers, are not yet fully integrated.

Appearance fidelity in single-image Real-to-Sim: Because Real-to-Sim compilation replaces visual elements with existing procedural assets, it cannot perfectly duplicate the exact geometry of source photograph items.
